name: Zoe Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Calder Electrical, a firm of about twenty that does rewires for the housing association, mostly old flats and terraced houses from the sixties. I'm in the van by seven with Gary, the older sparky I'm paired with, and we strip out old cable, chase walls, fit new consumer units and test everything before the tenants move back in. Sparky just means electrician, by the way. I like the bit at the end when you flick the main switch and every circuit tests clean.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The dust wears me out, and tenants who are scared because nobody told them we'd be cutting their power for a day. What I like is that it's real. Nobody can fake a test result on a ring circuit, it passes or it doesn't. I'm in the union, I live with my partner Theo, who drives buses, and I don't touch any of the AI stuff on my phone, I just don't trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the branch meeting I'd say the bosses spent a fortune on hype while our van fleet is falling apart. Online I'd probably just share some article laughing at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, which isn't the same as fine. The housing association contract comes up for renewal next spring and Calder is bidding against two cheaper firms. Our rent went up by 120 a month in August too, so I'm already watching every payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am, same van, same paperwork on the clipboard. I'd put an extra 100 a month into savings until the contract is signed, because we've got about three months put by and I'd like four. And I'd push the union rep to get the contract renewal on the agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with the old worry still sitting there. The AI going quiet doesn't make the rent or the contract go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Calder lost the housing association contract, what would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary says they'd keep the best two crews and let the rest go, and I'm not the best two crews, I'm the middle. There are other firms in town, so I'd find something, but maybe on worse terms or agency work. Agency means no sick pay, and Theo's shifts already change every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the AI stuff. Has anyone at Calder tried to bring it in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office tried an app that writes the test certificates from photos. I filled mine in by hand anyway, because if something burns down it's my name on that certificate, not the app's. My name on a certificate means something, and I'm not handing it to a phone.

say: I'd tell the union branch the **hype** cost money that should've gone on **vans and tools**.
I'd say online that real work like rewiring was never going to be **replaced by a chatbot**.
think: Nothing changing still leaves the **contract renewal** next spring hanging over my job.
Our **rent** jumped 120 a month, so even a normal year feels tight on **typical pay**.
do: Keep doing **rewires** the same way, with handwritten **test certificates**.
Put an extra **100 a month** into savings until the housing contract is signed.
Ask the **union rep** to raise the contract renewal at the next branch meeting.
feel: **Relieved** the hype faded, but still **uneasy** about the contract and the rent.
S0.quote: My name on a certificate means something, and I'm not handing it to a phone.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **not AI**: it's the housing association contract and a rent rise.
Refuses even small tools; her **signature on the certificate** is a point of pride and of legal duty.
Sits in the **middle of the crews**, so she knows she isn't the safest if the firm shrinks.

steps.text: Keep filling in rewire test certificates by hand
Save an extra 100 a month until the housing contract renews
Ask the union rep to put the contract renewal on the agenda

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: if the office gets AI, the savings should go to the workers, not the shareholders. At work I'd keep my head down, because the office staff would be the ones getting hit first. Online I'd be sharing every story about call centres closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my hands are safe for a while, it's the people around me I'd worry about. Sandra in the office books all our jobs and orders the cable, and that's exactly the stuff on your list. If the office shrinks, the bosses will want us to do the booking on a tablet ourselves, and I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on with the rewires and dig in. I'd go to every branch meeting and back any push for rules on how firms use AI. If they made us use a scheduling app I'd use it because I'd have to, but I wouldn't go and learn anything extra on my own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but I'd watch people I like lose theirs and I'd feel like the walls are closing in slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sandra if her job was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to come to the union with me, even though office staff aren't in our branch yet. And I'd probably cry with her in the car park, she's been there since before I started. Sandra ordered my first set of tools when I was an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people your age would jump at learning the new tools. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I learn the bosses' new system, it's so they can watch me more closely. The tracker in the van already tells the office when I stop for a coffee. I'd rather be good at the work than good at the bosses' apps.

say: I'd say any **AI savings** should be shared with **workers**, not shareholders.
Online I'd share stories of **office and call-centre jobs** being cut by AI.
think: My **hands-on work** is safe for now, but the **office staff** go first.
I expect the bosses to push **booking and ordering** onto electricians' tablets.
do: Attend every **union branch meeting** and back rules on AI at work.
Use any **scheduling app** only when forced, without learning extra on my own time.
Bring **Sandra** from the office to the union if her job is threatened.
feel: **Uneasy** watching colleagues lose work while her own job holds.
**Resentful** that each new app feels like more **monitoring**.
S1.quote: Every time I learn the bosses' new system, it's so they can watch me more closely.
fieldNote: Sees AI mostly as a **surveillance tool**; the van tracker colours everything.
Her strongest feeling is for **Sandra in the office**, not for herself.
Resistance is **principled**, not only fear: she won't give her own time to the firm's tools.

steps.text: Keep doing the housing association rewires with the same crew
Bring office staff like Sandra into the union
Back the union campaign for rules on AI at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, now, not after. At the branch I'd be pushing for a law that a licensed person has to sign off every installation. Online I'd be angry, I won't pretend I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years for the thinking stuff and five for robots is nothing. In 2028 Calder's office is gone, the quotes and the bookings and the certificates all done by the AI, and then by 2031 a robot is chasing walls in those flats. I'll be 32, with no other trade and no degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything big, we were going to put a deposit on a car and that would wait. I'd save every spare bit, aiming for six months instead of three. I'd join the campaign for the sign-off law, and I'd ask the union about any retraining fund, even though I hate the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. I'd be lying awake doing sums about Theo's wage on its own, and his job's on the list too with self-driving buses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about retraining even though you hate the idea. Into what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem, I don't know. Maybe care work, because robots doing that feels further off, or teaching apprentices while there still are any. I'd rather be fighting to keep my trade than picking a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Theo talk about the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit at the kitchen table with the bank app open and work out how long we'd last on one wage. Theo would say his buses will need drivers for years, and I'd say that's what Gary said about chasing walls. Two wages from two jobs that robots can do is not a plan.

say: I'd demand a law that a **licensed electrician** must sign off every **installation**.
I'd say openly that the **government** has to act now, not after the damage.
think: Two years for AI and **five for robots** leaves me with no time to change.
By **32** I'd have no other trade, and **Theo's bus job** is exposed too.
do: Put off the **car deposit** and cut big spending straight away.
Save hard to reach **six months** of expenses instead of three.
Ask the union about a **retraining fund**, possibly for care work.
feel: **Scared** and lying awake over whether the household could live on **one wage**.
S2.quote: Two wages from two jobs that robots can do is not a plan.
fieldNote: The **3-year robot gap** feels like no gap at all to her.
Household risk doubles: her partner **Theo drives buses**, which she also sees as exposed.
Even a resistant worker reaches for **retraining**, but only as a last resort.

steps.text: Put off the car deposit until the picture is clearer
Save toward six months of expenses instead of three
Campaign for a law that licensed electricians sign off installations
Ask the union about retraining funds for care work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say we need rules and a safety net, but I'd say it calmer. With five years there's time to organise properly. I'd tell the apprentices at Calder to get their full licences done fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI and eight to robots means I'd be about 35 when the robots really come. That's long enough to build a bit of a cushion, not long enough to feel safe. The thinking parts of my job, the paperwork, would go in 2031, and I'd be glad to see the back of that, if it didn't cost Sandra her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the rewires and save steadily, maybe 200 a month more. I'd get onto the union's AI working group so I'm not just shouting from the back. And I'd look into the inspection side, becoming the person who checks the robots' work, because someone still has to be legally responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less trapped. Seeing a storm on the horizon is better than having the storm on top of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned checking the robots' work. Is that a job you'd want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I want to wire houses. But inspection is still my trade, still my licence, and it keeps a human signature on the work. It's the version of change I could live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one I'd panic and spend the time scared. With five years I'd have time to sit the inspection course and let the union fight for the sign-off law. The fight matters more to me than any course.

say: I'd say there's **time to organise**, so we need rules and a safety net now.
I'd tell Calder's **apprentices** to finish their full **licences** quickly.
think: Robots arriving around **2034** means I'd be about **35**, with a small cushion built.
Losing the **paperwork** would suit me, but not if it costs office jobs.
do: Save about **200 a month** more while carrying on with rewires.
Join the union's **AI working group** instead of only complaining.
Look into an **inspection course** to stay the legally responsible person.
feel: **Anxious**, but less trapped, like seeing a **storm** coming from far off.
S3.quote: Seeing a storm on the horizon is better than having the storm on top of you.
fieldNote: More time turns her anger into **organising**: she joins the working group.
Inspection appeals because it keeps a **human signature** on the work, not because she likes desks.
Still expects her **income could shrink**, so the mood stays anxious, not uneasy.

steps.text: Save an extra 200 a month while still doing rewires
Join the union's working group on AI
Look into an electrical inspection course before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so no excuses for the government. I'd want the union to win guarantees now: retraining paid by the firms, and a human sign-off on every job. That's what I'd post, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 37 when the robots arrive in 2039. That's a long way off, and maybe I'd be running a crew by then. But I know myself, I'd put it off for nine years and then panic in the tenth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, not much. I'd keep rewiring, keep my savings ticking over, and get more active in the union. Maybe I'd start the inspection course in a few years, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. It feels far enough away that I can breathe, but I know that's a trap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What would make you act earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it on a site I know. If one of the big firms in town brought in a wall-chasing robot, I'd take it seriously that week. I don't believe headlines about robots, I believe what I see in a flat I'm rewiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Theo change any plans with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try to buy a flat in a few years, just a smaller one so the mortgage is something one of us could carry alone. Theo wants kids around 32, and I'd still want that too. Ten years is long enough to keep living.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough time, so the government has **no excuse**.
I'd push the union to win **firm-paid retraining** and human **sign-off** now.
think: Robots arriving in **2039** means I'd be **37**, maybe running a crew.
I know I'd **put it off** for nine years and then panic in the tenth.
do: Keep doing **rewires** and topping up savings at the **usual rate**.
Get more **active in the union** on retraining and sign-off rules.
Plan a **smaller flat** so one wage could carry the mortgage.
feel: **Able to breathe**, though she knows the calm could be a **trap**.
S4.quote: I don't believe headlines about robots, I believe what I see in a flat I'm rewiring.
fieldNote: She admits her own **habit of delay**, which is unusually honest.
Trusts only **what she sees**, not news or forecasts.
Long warning lets her **keep life plans**: a flat, maybe children around 32.

steps.text: Keep rewiring housing association flats with the same crew
Push the union for firm-paid retraining and human sign-off
Look for a smaller flat one wage could pay for

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years isn't time for anything, and it hits me and Theo both. What would help is a law that keeps a licensed person responsible for every installation, and a union strong enough to make firms pay for retraining instead of the government picking up the bill later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. In all of these, nobody's asking what the old woman in flat 4 thinks about a robot in her kitchen. Some of my tenants won't even let the gas man in without their daughter there.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be good at the work than good at the bosses' apps.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old union electrician** rewiring housing association flats for a firm of twenty.
She **refuses AI tools**, treating her signature on test certificates as a matter of **pride**.
Even in **AI Plateau** she worries about a contract renewal and a **rent rise**.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her because her partner Theo's **bus job** is exposed too.
With more time, her anger turns into **organising** and a reluctant look at **inspection** work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time and hits both wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** keeping a **licensed person** responsible for every installation.
A strong union that makes firms pay for **retraining**.
